CAS Monograph 15 is *Introduction to Capital Modeling and Portfolio
Management* (John Major and Stephen Mildenhall, 2026). It shows how an insurer
prices its risk and splits the price over its business units. The method uses
only a distribution of outcomes. The monograph's worked examples run in
Mildenhall's Python package `aggregate`. This guide runs them in prospicio from
R and prints the two sets of numbers side by side.

This is the R twin of the Python guide
[`capital-modeling-monograph-15.md`](capital-modeling-monograph-15.md), with
the same sections, examples and numbers. The R package calls the same Rust
code as the Python package. Thus the parameters, premiums and allocations
agree to every digit printed, and so do the Iman-Conover samples drawn by
seed.

The reasoning is the authors'. This guide explains it in new words and
recomputes the numbers. Read the monograph for the reasoning (chapters 3 to 6
and 8) and this guide for the mechanics (chapter 9). Table numbers are the
monograph's. Money is in the units of its examples.

The text block after each R chunk is the output of that chunk.
`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R` runs the chunks in order and checks that
each chunk prints exactly that text. To render the page, install the R package
(`remotes::install_github`, see `R/prospicio/bootstrap.R`) and run
`quarto render docs/guides/capital-modeling-monograph-15.qmd`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(prospicio)

# Thousands separators, as Python's {:,.0f}. Rounding first rounds a half to
# even, as Python does, on every platform's C library.
comma <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
}
```

## 1. The example company

The running example, InsCo, has three units, A, B and C, and ten equally
likely simulated years. Each row is a year, and each cell is the unit's loss in
that year:

```{r}
ROWS <- rbind(
  c(5, 20, 11), c(7, 33, 0), c(15, 13, 0), c(15, 7, 0), c(13, 20, 7),
  c(5, 27, 8), c(15, 16, 9), c(26, 19, 10), c(17, 8, 40), c(16, 20, 64)
)
colnames(ROWS) <- c("A", "B", "C")
insco <- capital_portfolio(ROWS)
totals <- rowSums(ROWS)

for (name in c("A", "B", "C", "Total")) {
  losses <- if (name == "Total") totals else ROWS[, name]
  s <- sampled(losses)
  sd <- sqrt(variance(s)) # sampled() divides by n, as the monograph does
  cat(sprintf("%-6s mean %6.2f  cv %.3f\n", name, mean(s), sd / mean(s)))
}
```

```text
A      mean  13.40  cv 0.453
B      mean  18.30  cv 0.412
C      mean  14.90  cv 1.324
Total  mean  46.60  cv 0.455
```

These are the last two rows of Table 9.1: means of 13.4, 18.3, 14.9 and 46.6,
and CVs of 0.453, 0.412, 1.324 and 0.455. Unit C is the volatile unit: it has a
small mean and a loss of 64 in the worst year.

`capital_portfolio()` takes the matrix of rows directly, with one named column
per unit. There is no frequency-severity model, no grid and no approximation.
Every number below comes from the ten years as they are.

Pricing works on the distinct totals, not on the years. Four years (the
second, fifth, sixth and seventh) each total 40. The portfolio keeps one
scenario at 40 with probability 0.4. For each unit, it keeps the average loss
at that total. The monograph calls this average the conditional expectation,
`kappa`. `portfolio_kappa(port, unit)` returns it for one unit, with one value
per distinct total (Python's `Portfolio.kappa(unit)`):

```{r}
cat("totals ", insco@totals, "\n")
cat("probs  ", round(insco@probs, 1), "\n")
for (unit in c("A", "B", "C")) {
  k <- portfolio_kappa(insco, unit) # E[X_unit | X = total]
  cat(sprintf("kappa %s", unit), sprintf("%.2f", k), "\n")
}
```

```text
totals  22 28 36 40 55 65 100
probs   0.1 0.1 0.1 0.4 0.1 0.1 0.1
kappa A 15.00 15.00 5.00 10.00 26.00 17.00 16.00
kappa B 7.00 13.00 20.00 24.00 19.00 8.00 20.00
kappa C 0.00 0.00 11.00 6.00 10.00 40.00 64.00
```

At a total of 40, the expected losses are 10 for A, 24 for B and 6 for C.
This is the row of Table 9.4. The conditional expectations always add up to the
total. Thus a split of the price by them never creates or loses money.

## 2. The capital standard

A price needs a capital standard: the assets that stand behind the book.
Chapter 3 of the monograph defines value at risk (VaR, a quantile) and tail
value at risk (TVaR, the average above that quantile). `aggregate` and
prospicio read a standard of "p" as assets equal to the p quantile of the
total. `portfolio_assets(port, p)` (Python's `Portfolio.assets(p)`) gives this
level. `natural_price(port, d, p = p)` prices at this level for any distortion
`d`:

```{r}
total <- sampled(totals)
cat(sprintf("%5s %6s %8s  assets at p\n", "p", "VaR", "TVaR"))
for (p in c(0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 1.0)) {
  cat(sprintf("%5.2f %6.0f %8.3f  %.0f\n", p, quantile(total, p), TVaR(total, p),
              portfolio_assets(insco, p)))
}
```

```text
    p    VaR     TVaR  assets at p
 0.80     55   82.500  55
 0.85     65   88.333  65
 0.90     65  100.000  65
 1.00    100  100.000  100
```

These values are Table 9.5. With ten years, the 100% standard is the worst
year, and TVaR is 100 from 90% up. Thus the main example of the monograph uses
full capitalization: assets of 100, the largest loss. With ten scenarios, a
99.5% standard also gives the worst year, so the example uses the simplest
standard.

## 3. Calibrating five distortions

The monograph prices with a **distortion** (a spectral risk measure). A
distortion is a function `g` that increases the probability of bad outcomes.
The price is the expected loss under these increased probabilities.

You choose a distortion from a family and then calibrate it. Here the
calibration has one requirement: the whole book earns a 15% return on capital,
with assets of 100. The expected loss is 46.6. Thus the premium `P` and the
capital `Q = 100 - P` must satisfy `P - 46.6 = 0.15 Q`, which gives
`P = 53.565`.

Five families each have one parameter: constant cost of capital (CCoC),
proportional hazard (PH), Wang, dual power and TVaR. `calibrate_portfolio()`
finds the parameter value that gives that premium:

```{r}
FAMILIES <- c("ccoc", "ph", "wang", "dual", "tvar")
distortions <- lapply(stats::setNames(FAMILIES, FAMILIES), function(family) {
  calibrate_portfolio(insco, family, assets = 100, return_on_capital = 0.15)
})
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  value <- distortions[[family]]@parameters
  cat(sprintf("%-5s %-7s %.3f\n", family, names(value), value))
}
```

```text
ccoc  r       0.150
ph    rho     0.720
wang  lambda  0.343
dual  beta    1.595
tvar  p       0.271
```

Table 9.3 prints 0.150, 0.720, 0.343, 1.595 and 0.271 for these parameters.
The values agree. The CCoC parameter has a different meaning in each program.
`aggregate` builds the CCoC distortion from a risk discount
`d = 0.15 / 1.15`, and prospicio builds it from the cost of capital `r = 0.15`.
`distortion("ccoc", 0.15)` is the same function.

## 4. The price and its allocation to units

After calibration, `natural_price()` returns the premium of the loss capped at
the assets. It also returns the **natural allocation** of that premium to the
units, as a data frame with one row per unit and a `"total"` row. Each unit
pays the distorted average of its own loss in the bad years. Thus a unit that
loses most when the total is large pays more. With `allocation = "linear"`,
`natural_price()` also splits the assets by expected shares above the asset
level.

```{r}
BOOK_LINEAR <- c(A = 13.739, B = 18.522, C = 21.304) # Table 9.6 for CCoC: premium by unit
priced <- natural_price(insco, distortions$ccoc, assets = 100, allocation = "linear")
cat(sprintf("%-6s %7s %7s %7s %7s %7s %6s\n", "", "L", "a", "Q", "P", "M", "COC"))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(priced))) {
  u <- priced[i, ]
  name <- if (u$unit == "total") "Total" else u$unit
  margin <- u$premium - u$loss
  cat(sprintf("%-6s %7.3f %7.3f %7.3f %7.3f %7.3f %6.3f\n", name, u$loss, u$assets,
              u$capital, u$premium, margin, margin / u$capital))
}
```

```text
             L       a       Q       P       M    COC
A       13.400  16.000   2.261  13.739   0.339  0.150
B       18.300  20.000   1.478  18.522   0.222  0.150
C       14.900  64.000  42.696  21.304   6.404  0.150
Total   46.600 100.000  46.435  53.565   6.965  0.150
```

This is Table 9.6, the "industry standard" CCoC pricing. Every unit earns 15%
on its allocated capital, because this allocation defines capital that way.
Unit C takes 64 of the 100 of assets. It pays 21.3 of the premium for an
expected loss of 14.9, so C has most of the margin (6.4 of 7.0). The unit
premiums add up to the book's 53.565.

The data frame also has the columns `margin`, `loss_ratio` and
`return_on_capital`. The chunk calculates the margin and its return by hand to
show their source.

The five distortions give the same total premium, because the calibration sets
it. The distortions differ in which unit pays. Table 9.8 of the monograph
shows the premiums by unit, and they agree here:

```{r}
BOOK_P <- list( # Table 9.8, premium by unit (A, B, C)
  ccoc = c(13.739, 18.522, 21.304),
  ph = c(14.060, 18.349, 21.156),
  wang = c(14.109, 18.637, 20.819),
  dual = c(14.127, 19.117, 20.322),
  tvar = c(13.783, 20.412, 19.371)
)
units_only <- function(priced) priced[priced$unit != "total", ]
cat(sprintf("%-5s %20s %20s %20s\n", "", "A", "B", "C"))
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  got <- units_only(natural_price(insco, distortions[[family]], assets = 100))$premium
  cells <- sprintf("%7.3f (book %6.3f)", got, BOOK_P[[family]])
  cat(sprintf("%-5s ", family), paste(cells, collapse = " "), "\n", sep = "")
}
```

```text
                         A                    B                    C
ccoc   13.739 (book 13.739)  18.522 (book 18.522)  21.304 (book 21.304)
ph     14.060 (book 14.060)  18.349 (book 18.349)  21.156 (book 21.156)
wang   14.109 (book 14.109)  18.637 (book 18.637)  20.819 (book 20.819)
dual   14.127 (book 14.127)  19.117 (book 19.117)  20.322 (book 20.322)
tvar   13.783 (book 13.783)  20.412 (book 20.412)  19.371 (book 19.371)
```

All fifteen premiums match to the three decimals printed. The pattern across
the rows is the important result. CCoC prices unit C at 21.3 and unit B at
18.5. TVaR prices B at 20.4 and C at 19.4.

TVaR charges only for the units' losses in the worst years. In those years,
B's 20 is a larger share of the total than its average share. CCoC charges for
the volume of capital that each unit uses, and C uses 64 of the 100. Neither
distortion is the right answer. The distortion states what you are paid to
bear (see [Risk loads and distortions](risk-loads-and-distortions.md)).

## 5. Capital by unit, if you must

Section 8.3 of the monograph advises against capital allocation, because
layers of capital cost different amounts. It allocates margin instead. To
state the capital that each unit uses, the monograph gives a method. The
method allocates each layer of the asset range by the units' shares of that
layer's margin, and then adds the layers. In prospicio this is
`allocation = "lifted"`:

```{r}
BOOK_Q <- list( # Table 9.8, capital by unit (A, B, C)
  ccoc = c(4.874, 5.288, 36.273),
  ph = c(7.074, 6.565, 32.796),
  wang = c(8.411, 8.691, 29.333),
  dual = c(8.873, 9.143, 28.419),
  tvar = c(9.034, 9.247, 28.154)
)
cat(sprintf("%-5s %20s %20s %20s\n", "", "A", "B", "C"))
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  lifted <- natural_price(insco, distortions[[family]], assets = 100, allocation = "lifted")
  cells <- sprintf("%7.3f (book %6.3f)", units_only(lifted)$capital, BOOK_Q[[family]])
  cat(sprintf("%-5s ", family), paste(cells, collapse = " "), "\n", sep = "")
}
```

```text
                         A                    B                    C
ccoc    2.261 (book  4.874)   1.478 (book  5.288)  42.696 (book 36.273)
ph      6.481 (book  7.074)   5.597 (book  6.565)  34.356 (book 32.796)
wang    8.411 (book  8.411)   8.691 (book  8.691)  29.333 (book 29.333)
dual    8.873 (book  8.873)   9.143 (book  9.143)  28.419 (book 28.419)
tvar    9.034 (book  9.034)   9.247 (book  9.247)  28.154 (book 28.154)
```

Wang, dual power and TVaR agree with the monograph to three decimals. **CCoC
and PH do not agree.** For CCoC, the monograph prints 4.874, 5.288 and 36.273.
prospicio gives 2.261, 1.478 and 42.696, the same as the linear allocation.
For PH, the monograph prints 7.074, 6.565 and 32.796, and prospicio gives
6.481, 5.597 and 34.356. The premiums and margins are the same. Only the split
of capital between units differs.

The difference comes from the `aggregate` version. The monograph's code ran on
`aggregate` 0.24.0, and `aggregate` 0.30.1 prints the monograph's values.
`aggregate` 1.0.1 gives prospicio's values. CI checks prospicio against
`aggregate` 1.0.1 on InsCo at 1e-10, for both allocations and all five
distortions.

The monograph's own argument also gives prospicio's CCoC value. Under CCoC,
every layer of capital earns 15%, so a unit's capital is its margin divided by
0.15. Unit A's margin of 0.339 gives 2.261. Use the premiums and margins, which
agree in all versions. Capital by unit under CCoC and PH depends on the
version.

## 6. The reinsurance decision

Chapter 5 asks how a reinsurance cover changes the price of the book. The
example is an aggregate stop loss of 35 excess of 65. The reinsurer pays the
amount by which the year's total exceeds 65, up to 35. On these ten years it
pays in one year only, the year of 100. The recovery is 35 with probability
0.1, a mean of 3.5.

Make the recovery and the net loss two units of a new portfolio. This
portfolio prices the cover and shows what the retained book needs:

```{r}
stop_loss <- function(total, attach = 65, limit = 35) pmin(pmax(total - attach, 0), limit)

split <- cbind(Net = totals - stop_loss(totals), Ceded = stop_loss(totals))
reinsured <- capital_portfolio(split)
cat("means", reinsured@expected, " (book: net 43.1, ceded 3.5)\n")

BOOK_RE <- list( # Table 9.10, premium and margin of ceded and net, (ceded, net)
  ccoc = c(7.609, 4.109, 45.957, 2.857),
  ph = c(6.662, 3.162, 46.903, 3.803),
  wang = c(6.087, 2.587, 47.478, 4.378),
  dual = c(5.415, 1.915, 48.151, 5.051),
  tvar = c(4.803, 1.303, 48.762, 5.662)
)
cat(sprintf("%-5s %8s %7s %8s %7s\n", "", "ceded P", "M", "net P", "M"))
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  r <- natural_price(reinsured, distortions[[family]], assets = 100)
  ceded <- r[r$unit == "Ceded", ]
  net <- r[r$unit == "Net", ]
  cat(sprintf("%-5s %8.3f %7.3f %8.3f %7.3f   book %s\n", family,
              ceded$premium, ceded$premium - ceded$loss, net$premium, net$premium - net$loss,
              paste(sprintf("%.3f", BOOK_RE[[family]]), collapse = " ")))
}
```

```text
means 43.1 3.5  (book: net 43.1, ceded 3.5)
       ceded P       M    net P       M
ccoc     7.609   4.109   45.957   2.857   book 7.609 4.109 45.957 2.857
ph       6.662   3.162   46.903   3.803   book 6.662 3.162 46.903 3.803
wang     6.087   2.587   47.478   4.378   book 6.087 2.587 47.478 4.378
dual     5.415   1.915   48.151   5.051   book 5.415 1.915 48.151 5.051
tvar     4.803   1.303   48.762   5.662   book 4.803 1.303 48.762 5.662
```

The reinsurer's price depends strongly on the distortion. The cover protects
only against the worst year, so the risk loads are in the tail. CCoC prices
the cover at 7.609, a margin of 4.109, which is more than the expected loss of
3.5. Dual power prices it at 5.415.

Chapter 6 of the monograph asks which distortion is the right measure for the
reinsurer's price, or for the buyer's willingness to pay. The method gives the
answer for every distortion on one page. The two margins always add up to the
book's 6.965. Thus a more expensive cover (CCoC) leaves less margin for the
retained book (2.857) than a less expensive cover (dual power leaves 5.051).

## 7. A more realistic example

The last section of chapter 9 builds a book from frequency and severity. The
book has three units, Auto, GL and WC. Each unit has a lognormal severity with
a per-claim limit and a gamma-mixed Poisson count, compounded by FFT.
Iman-Conover rank correlation then ties the units together. The monograph
prices the book at a 99.5% standard and a 15% return.

In R, a unit uses these functions:

1. `discretize()` with the local moment method.
2. `map_grid()` for the per-claim limit.
3. `mixed_poisson_count()` for the count.
4. `compound_distribution(..., method = "fft")`, whose grid keeps the FFT's
   checks in its `report`.

```{r}
compound_unit <- function(loss, limit, mean, cv, mixing_cv, step, points) {
  # A unit: expected loss, a per-claim limit, a lognormal, a gamma mixed count.
  severity <- discretize(lognormal_from_mean_cv(mean, cv), step, points, "local_moment")
  claim <- map_grid(severity, function(x) pmin(x, limit))$grid
  claims <- loss / mean(claim)
  annual <- compound_distribution(mixed_poisson_count(claims, mixing_cv), claim, points,
                                  method = "fft")
  list(claims = claims, claim_mean = mean(claim), annual = annual, report = annual@report)
}

UNITS <- list(
  Auto = list(5000, 5000, 50, 2.0, 0.2, 0.25, 2^16),
  GL = list(3000, 2500, 75, 3.0, 0.3, 0.25, 2^16),
  WC = list(7000, 25000, 5, 10.0, 0.25, 0.25, 2^17)
)
annual <- list()
cat(sprintf("%-5s %8s %11s %9s %7s %10s\n", "", "claims", "claim mean", "agg mean",
            "agg cv", "tail mass"))
for (name in names(UNITS)) {
  unit <- do.call(compound_unit, UNITS[[name]])
  a <- annual[[name]] <- unit$annual
  cat(sprintf("%-5s %8.1f %11.3f %9.1f %7.3f %10.1e\n", name, unit$claims, unit$claim_mean,
              mean(a), sqrt(variance(a)) / mean(a), unit$report$tail_mass))
}
```

```text
        claims  claim mean  agg mean  agg cv  tail mass
Auto     100.0      49.982    5000.0   0.298    2.3e-06
GL        41.0      73.156    3000.0   0.502    4.4e-07
WC      1401.1       4.996    6999.7   0.349    1.6e-04
```

Table 9.11 of the monograph prints 100.0, 41.008 and 1,401.1 claims, and mean
claims of 49.982, 73.156 and 4.996 (4.945 on its grid). It prints aggregate
CVs of 0.298, 0.502 and 0.349. The numbers agree. Unit WC drives the tail,
with a thick-tailed severity and a high limit.

Iman-Conover pairs the units' draws so that their rank correlations match a
target. It does not change the distribution of any unit. The code below does
these steps:

1. Draw each unit at evenly spaced quantiles.
2. Tie the draws with the monograph's matrix (Table 9.12). `iman_conover()`
   does this on a `predictive_distribution()` with one component per unit.
3. Build a portfolio from the result with `capital_portfolio()`. It reads each
   simulation as an equally likely scenario (Python's
   `Portfolio.from_predictive`).

```{r}
TARGET <- rbind(c(1.0, 0.5, 0.4), c(0.5, 1.0, 0.1), c(0.4, 0.1, 1.0))

correlated_portfolio <- function(n_sims, seed) {
  q <- (seq_len(n_sims) - 0.5) / n_sims
  draws <- sapply(annual, function(g) quantile(g, q)) # n_sims rows, one column per unit
  keys <- data.frame(unit = names(annual))
  joint <- iman_conover(predictive_distribution(draws, keys), TARGET, seed)
  capital_portfolio(joint)
}

book <- correlated_portfolio(50000, 4817)
cat("units", book@units, " means", sprintf("%.1f", book@expected), "\n")
```

```text
units Auto GL WC  means 5000.0 3000.0 6999.7
```

Now calibrate the five distortions to a 15% return at the 99.5% standard
(Table 9.16), and price each unit (Table 9.17):

```{r}
BOOK_PARAMS <- c(ccoc = 0.150, ph = 0.654, wang = 0.437, dual = 1.756, tvar = 0.299)
priced_book <- list()
cat(sprintf("assets at 99.5%%: %s   (book 28,898)\n", comma(portfolio_assets(book, 0.995))))
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  d <- calibrate_portfolio(book, family, p = 0.995, return_on_capital = 0.15)
  pb <- priced_book[[family]] <- natural_price(book, d, p = 0.995)
  cells <- paste(sprintf("%8.1f", units_only(pb)$premium), collapse = " ")
  cat(sprintf("%-5s parameter %.3f (book %.3f)   premium Auto, GL, WC: %s   total %s\n",
              family, d@parameters, BOOK_PARAMS[[family]], cells,
              comma(pb$premium[pb$unit == "total"], 1)))
}
```

```text
assets at 99.5%: 28,448   (book 28,898)
ccoc  parameter 0.150 (book 0.150)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5351.0   3230.1   8154.6   total 16,735.8
ph    parameter 0.654 (book 0.654)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5483.4   3377.8   7874.6   total 16,735.8
wang  parameter 0.434 (book 0.437)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5511.0   3405.1   7819.6   total 16,735.8
dual  parameter 1.740 (book 1.756)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5529.0   3421.1   7785.6   total 16,735.8
tvar  parameter 0.291 (book 0.299)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5536.0   3423.9   7776.0   total 16,735.8
```

The parameters are within about 0.01 of Table 9.16. The PH parameter is equal,
and the TVaR level is 0.291 against 0.299. The total premium of about 16,740 is
close to the monograph's 16,800.3.

Exact agreement is not expected. The monograph's sample has 1,000
simulations, so its 99.5% quantile rests on five points. The draws here are
50,000 and evenly spaced. To see how much a sample of 1,000 moves the answer,
run the same calculation on samples of different sizes:

```{r}
for (run in list(c(1000, 11), c(1000, 12), c(10000, 11), c(50000, 11))) {
  pf <- correlated_portfolio(run[1], run[2])
  d <- calibrate_portfolio(pf, "ccoc", p = 0.995, return_on_capital = 0.15)
  p <- natural_price(pf, d, p = 0.995)
  tot <- p[p$unit == "total", ]
  cat(sprintf("%6d sims, seed %d: assets %9s  premium %9s\n", run[1], run[2],
              comma(tot$assets), comma(tot$premium, 1)))
}
```

```text
  1000 sims, seed 11: assets    27,850  premium  16,657.6
  1000 sims, seed 12: assets    29,368  premium  16,855.1
 10000 sims, seed 11: assets    28,692  premium  16,771.1
 50000 sims, seed 11: assets    28,520  premium  16,744.9
```

The premium moves by one or two percent between two samples of 1,000, and it
settles as the sample grows. Thus do not quote numbers from a small sample to
four digits. For more units, more events and a real model, the monograph
gives the same advice. Use more simulations and a capital standard that you
can defend.

The seeded samples are the same in R and Python. `iman_conover()` runs the
same Rust code from the same seed. Thus these four lines and the table above
are equal to the Python guide's. The assets of the second sample are exactly
29,368.5. The `comma()` helper of the setup chunk rounds that half to even, as
Python does. R's `sprintf("%.0f", 29368.5)` prints 29369 on Windows and 29368
on Linux.
